segments.text: In 2019, Facebook was fined five billion dollars. The largest penalty in FTC history. Eighty-seven million people's data — harvested, profiled, and sold to a political targeting firm without their knowledge. And on the day the fine was announced, Facebook's stock went up. The market added six billion dollars in value. Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day. The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.

segments.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions. They had the crash test data. Two engineers wrote a cost-benefit analysis — an actual document, with actual numbers. Fix every Pinto: one hundred and thirty-seven million dollars. Expected wrongful death payouts: forty-nine point five million. They shipped the car.
segments.notes: Recall notice is the perfect documentary anchor — a physical document the company produced. Zoom target on document so viewer knows this is real paperwork, not illustration. Lower-third establishes company and year context immediately.

segments.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino. The fuel tank ruptured. The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. Burned over his entire body. Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. A childhood replaced by hospital rooms. The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history. The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide. No executive went to prison.

sfx.motivation: crash impact — the moment the Pinto burns with a child inside

segments.notes: Half-beat before the name 'Richard Grimshaw' — humanize before the horror. Glass shatter on the cut to fire image makes the collision visceral. This is the first real emotional anchor of the film. Keep music low here.

segments.text: The fine was three point five million dollars. Ford kept selling cars. No one went to prison. And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something. The cost of getting caught was less than the cost of doing the right thing.

sfx.motivation: revelation impact — fine announced, no one goes to prison

segments.notes: Full 1s pause before 'The fine was three point five million' — the viewer needs to brace. Impact SFX as the dollar number appears. Court case document legitimizes the number. 'No one went to prison' lands harder after this visual setup.

segments.text: That might have been an isolated scandal. A single bad company making a single bad calculation. Except it wasn't.
segments.notes: Deliberate energy drop after the revelation — aftermath beat. Boardroom image is cold and generic, representing 'any company.' The dissolve out signals a pivot to the next story. 'Except it wasn't' is the hook into Wells Fargo.

segments.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. She told the truth. She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission. She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products. "Eight is Great." Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired. So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment.
segments.notes: Half-beat pause signals a new character is being introduced. Ethics hotline image is the key visual — it's the object Yesenia will use, and it's about to be shown as a trap. Lower-third anchors the new case study. Dissolve in from aftermath energy.

segments.text: Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud. Wells Fargo terminated her the same week. She never found steady work in banking again. Her name went on an industry blacklist — a record that follows you like a scar.

sfx.motivation: emotional impact — whistleblower fired the same week she reported

segments.notes: Full 1s pause before 'Wells Fargo terminated her the same week.' Impact SFX makes the firing land as a physical blow. Dramatic silhouette is deliberately anonymous — Yesenia represents every whistleblower who gets crushed. No name overlay here; let the narration carry the emotion.

segments.text: Three point five million fake accounts. Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them. And the woman who designed the quota — Carrie Tolstedt, head of Community Banking — kept fifty-seven million dollars and got zero prison time. She served her sentence at home. Ford's formula required a memo. Wells Fargo's didn't even require a decision — just a number and a threat.

segments.notes: Glass shatter on the number — 3.5 million is the shattering fact. Executive image contrasts with Yesenia's silhouette: she lost her job, they kept theirs. Stat overlay makes the scale impossible to ignore. 'The woman who exposed it' gets no justice — let that land on the executive's face.

segments.text: Ford needed a document to do this. Wells Fargo only needed a quota. The next company didn't need either. It just needed a head start.
segments.notes: Deliberate cooldown — this is the analytical beat where we connect Ford and Wells Fargo. Financial spreadsheet evokes 'the calculation' — the formula being built piece by piece. 'Ford needed a document. Wells Fargo only needed a quota.' The spreadsheet IS the quota.

segments.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early and withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before anyone could calculate the fine. Richard Sackler promised a, quote, blizzard of prescriptions at OxyContin's launch. In Kermit, West Virginia — population four hundred — a single pharmacy received nine million opioid pills in two years. The pharmacist went to prison. The Sacklers moved their money. More than eight hundred thousand Americans died. The settlement: seven point four billion. The family's remaining fortune: thirteen billion. Nine thousand dollars per death. Ford valued a life at two hundred thousand in 1977. The Sacklers got it down to nine thousand.

sfx.motivation: shock at preemptive asset withdrawal — Purdue took the money BEFORE paying the fine

segments.notes: Stacked money image makes the abstraction concrete. Impact SFX on the stat. The key detail is 'a decade early' — they saw the settlement coming and legally looted the company first. Dissolve out leads into the thesis PAUSE. Begin music fade here.

segments.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.

segments.text: And the price keeps dropping. Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone. One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than a billion. And here's the number that should end every argument about whether the system works: companies caught repeatedly pay smaller fines as a percentage of their revenue over time. Not larger. Smaller. The more you violate, the better the deal gets.
segments.notes: Dissolve in — deliberate energy drop after the thesis peak. This is the data backing the thesis. Bar chart with the $1T overlay makes the scale undeniable. Narration becomes analytical here — the viewer has been emotionally hit, now they get the receipts.

segments.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation. Ford added a memo. Wells Fargo added plausible deniability. Purdue added preemption. Facebook added scale. But every one of them had something in common — the damage, at least in theory, could be reversed. Ford could recall the car. Wells Fargo could close the accounts. Purdue could stop making the pills.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]

segments.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app. Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it. But Facebook's API — the system that connects apps to the platform — gave the quiz access to not just those users' data, but all of their friends' data too. Every like, every post, every photo, every connection. Two hundred and seventy thousand downloads became eighty-seven million people's data harvested in weeks.
segments.notes: Forum/social post image evokes the quiz environment — the trap. The 270K→87M stat overlay is the key escalation: the quiz was the tip, the friend network was the spear. This is the mechanism. Keep energy moderate — the revelation comes next.

segments.text: Facebook knew this was possible. It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive engagement, and engagement drives advertising revenue. In 2014, they quietly changed the rules. But they never enforced deletion of the data already taken.

sfx.motivation: revelation — Facebook designed the API to be open ON PURPOSE

segments.notes: Glass shatter on the cut as 'feature, not a bug' lands. Different server image from seg 18 — this one is colder, more clinical. The reveal that Facebook INTENTIONALLY built the exploit into the API is the pivot. Wide servers evoke the inhuman scale of the surveillance architecture.

segments.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you felt it. They were hired by the Trump campaign. They were hired by groups supporting Brexit.
segments.notes: AI/data processing image evokes Cambridge Analytica's modelling operation. 'Voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you knew yourself' — this is manipulation at industrial scale. Keep energy high but don't SFX here; save the hit for seg 25.

segments.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities — measured, modeled, and weaponized — for the price of a free quiz they never took. And most of them still don't know. A 2019 Pew survey found that seventy-four percent of Facebook users didn't know the platform maintained a list of their interests and traits for ad targeting. They didn't know they'd been profiled. They didn't know their data had been sold. They just knew that their feed felt different in 2016 — angrier, more anxious, more polarized — and they assumed that was the world changing. It wasn't the world. It was the algorithm. Tuned by their own data, sold without their consent, deployed to shape an election.

sfx.motivation: emotional peak — 87 million human personalities measured, modeled, weaponized

segments.notes: Full 1s pause. Loud glass shatter on the number. This is the human cost made visceral — 87 million silhouettes compressed into one. Different silhouette image from seg 9 (this is the second use pattern, not a repeat). Music rises. '...for the price of a free quiz they never consented to' should land in silence after the music swell.

segments.text: When the story broke in March 2018, Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress. He wore a suit. He said sorry. And then something happened that tells you everything about why the formula survives.
segments.notes: Deliberate energy drop into aftermath. Capitol footage grounds the congressional hearing in physical space. Mute clip audio — we're in VO narration mode. Dissolve in from the 87M emotional peak. Lower-third signals the time jump. 'He wore a suit. He said sorry.' is dry and sardonic — the cool wide shot matches that tone.

Music returns and builds — we're heading into the next section. Dissolve out signals the story isn't over. The comedy was the cover.

segments.text: But here's what nobody said at the time. That hearing was the formula protecting itself. The people who set the fines — who write the regulations, who are supposed to be the ceiling on corporate behavior — didn't understand the business model of the company they were interrogating. And Zuckerberg knew it. He sat there, patient and composed, and explained his own business to the people who were supposed to be punishing him. He wasn't being grilled. He was giving a tutorial. And everyone watched it happen and laughed — because it was easier to laugh than to realize what it meant.

segments.notes: Hard cut from Zuckerberg face to abstracted formula visual. Impact SFX punctuates the reframe. Typewriter text echoes the thesis. Music swells briefly then drops back under VO.

segments.text: The FTC investigated for over a year. In July 2019, they announced the largest fine in their history: five billion dollars.

segments.text: Here is what five billion dollars means to Facebook. Revenue that year: seventy point seven billion. The fine was seven percent. Net profit: eighteen point five billion. The fine was about twenty-seven percent of one year's profit — paid once, for a violation that ran for years and compromised eighty-seven million people.
segments.notes: Static text overlay renders the math visible as narrator speaks it. Stays on screen for the duration of the revenue comparison — viewers should see the percentage while hearing it.

The market's verdict was clear: this is the ceiling. This is the worst it gets. And the worst it gets is a good day.

segments.text: Now. After everything I've just shown you — Ford, Wells Fargo, Purdue, Facebook — you'd be forgiven for thinking the formula is unbeatable. That this is just how it works. Fine, settle, move on. Nobody learns. Nothing changes.

segments.text: Within weeks, they rewrote their entire data transfer infrastructure. They shut down a pipeline they'd run for a decade. They rebuilt their European architecture from scratch. They didn't fight it in court for years. They didn't issue a press release and wait for it to blow over. They fixed it. Immediately. Because for the first time, the violation was more expensive than the profit.

segments.text: Sit with that for a second. The formula — the one that has survived five decades, across every industry, through every administration — broke. In Europe. Because someone changed one variable: they made the fine proportional.

segments.text: When Ford got caught, they could recall the car. When Facebook got caught, they could — in theory — delete the data. When Purdue got caught, they could stop manufacturing the pills. The damage was reversible. Expensive, slow, and nobody ever did it voluntarily. But the off switch existed.

segments.text: With AI, there is no off switch. When a model trains on scraped data, that data dissolves into the model's parameters like sugar dissolved in water. You cannot un-dissolve it. You cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs. You cannot point to a sentence and say "that came from Reddit" or "that came from a children's book published in 2019." The data becomes the model. The violation becomes the product. Every response the AI generates, every image it creates, every answer it provides — built on content taken without permission and impossible to return.

A publisher she'd worked with for two years emailed to say they were "exploring AI-generated options" for their next cover. Her commissions dropped. Her online sales fell. The style she'd spent a decade developing could now be approximated in seconds by typing a sentence into a box. She started pivoting to 3D art — not because she wanted to, but because she hoped three-dimensional work would be harder to scrape.

segments.text: Chris Vialpondo is a renter in Seattle's Lower Queen Anne neighborhood. In 2022, he opened a notice from his property manager and learned his rent had increased by fifty percent. Same apartment. Same neighborhood. Same job. He was already working two jobs to make rent. Fifty percent meant the difference between getting by and going under. It meant counting every grocery trip. It meant the constant math of which bill gets paid this week and which one waits. He reached out to his property manager — the human being he thought had set the price — and was told nothing could be done. Because his property manager hadn't set the price. A company he'd never heard of had.

segments.text: RealPage. A company that takes confidential pricing data from competing landlords — data that competitors are not legally supposed to share — and feeds it into an algorithm that recommends rent prices across more than thirteen million apartments. Ninety percent of landlords follow the recommendation. The result: coordinated rent increases across buildings that are supposed to be competing with each other. The Department of Justice found that the algorithm costs renters an average of seventy dollars a month more — and over a hundred dollars a month in six major metro areas.

segments.text: Europe figured this out. Four percent of global revenue. Proportional. Automatic. No ceiling. When the fine scales with the company, the formula breaks. Facebook shrugged off a five-billion-dollar American fine and panicked over a European one. The tools exist. Criminal liability for executives — not the tellers, the architects. Disgorgement — hand back every dollar earned from the violation, not a negotiated fraction. The legal frameworks are built. The question has never been how. The question is why.

segments.text: And the answer is the same math that runs everything else in this video. The companies that benefit from the formula fund the campaigns, staff the advisory boards, draft the legislation. The fine stays small because the people who pay it set the ceiling.
